planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring directly into saturated, acidic muck at a bog or pond margin; tufted loosestrife spreads by rhizomes and tolerates standing water a few inches deep.

directions: Set out divisions in consistently saturated, mucky soil at the edge of a bog, fen, or pond, since this species will not persist where the root zone dries out between rains. Unusual fuzzy yellow flower spikes emerge sideways from the leaf axils rather than the stem tip in early summer, a trait that distinguishes it from other loosestrifes. It colonizes slowly by shallow rhizomes, so give it room to form a spreading colony rather than treating it as a single clump. Cut back old stems in late winter to tidy the planting before new shoots emerge.

planting.note: Plant into constantly wet, acidic, peaty soil typical of sphagnum bogs, sedge meadows, and the shaded margins of conifer swamps; keep roots saturated through the growing season.

directions: This bog specialist needs ground that stays saturated all season, with red-veined stems and blue-green foliage marking it even before the small pink, short-lived flowers open in mid to late summer. It is naturally found growing in the dappled light under alder thickets and at conifer swamp edges as readily as in full sun, so a partly shaded bog garden suits it well. Because it dislikes competition and drying out, plant it where sphagnum or other low moss can keep the surrounding soil consistently damp. Divide congested clumps every few years in early spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into permanently moist to wet, acidic soil; bog birch is a classic fen and bog-margin shrub and resents drying out even briefly once established.

directions: Bog birch is a many-stemmed, rounded shrub rather than a tree, with small round leaves and catkins that make it easy to mistake for a tall shrubby willow at a glance. It forms thickets at the shrubby margins between open sedge fens and surrounding forest, tolerating open sun but also some shade from neighboring conifers. Give it continuously saturated to consistently moist, cold, acidic soil, since it is one of the most cold-hardy native birches and struggles in average garden conditions. Use it to anchor the woody edge of a rain garden or constructed bog rather than a conventional shrub border.

planting.note: Divide clumps or plant plugs in spring into wet, calcium-rich soil typical of grassy fens and sedge meadows; tolerates brief flooding and standing water.

directions: Named for the bristly, barbed seed heads that look faintly spiky up close, this fen sedge forms arching, grass-like clumps that add texture to a wet meadow or restored calcareous fen planting. It wants wet, often calcium-enriched soil and open light, the conditions found in the grassy fens and marsh edges where it grows naturally alongside sedges and rushes. Because its seed heads droop and rattle attractively in fall, leave stems standing through winter for seed-eating birds and cut back old growth only in early spring. Division of established clumps is the most reliable way to multiply it for a new planting.
